title: Stalks of a constant sheaf on the pro-etale site
statement: Let $Y$ be a scheme with small pro-etale site $Y_{\mathrm{proet}}$ [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], let $\Lambda$ be a commutative ring, $M$ a $\Lambda$-module, and $\underline M_Y$ the constant sheaf of $\Lambda_Y$-modules on $Y_{\mathrm{proet}}$, the sheafification of the constant presheaf $U\mapsto M$ [def-weil-proetale-locally-constant-sheaf]. Let $\bar y:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to Y$ be a geometric point and $(\underline M_Y)_{\bar y}$ the stalk of $\underline M_Y$ at $\bar y$, the colimit of sections over the pointed neighbourhoods of $\bar y$ in $Y_{\mathrm{proet}}$ [def-weil-proetale-geometric-stalk]. Then the canonical map $M\to(\underline M_Y)_{\bar y}$ (sending $m$ to the germ at $(Y,\bar y)$ of the image of the constant section $m$) is an isomorphism of $\Lambda$-modules. In particular, if $M$ is finite, every stalk of $\underline M_Y$ at a geometric point is finite.

source.place: used without statement: p. 58, Lemma 6.8.2 and Definition 6.8.3, and p. 49, §6.5 (constant sheaves $\underline L$ pulled back from $D(R)$); the two facts behind it are that sheafification does not change stalks (literature/stacks-project/sites.tex, Lemma 'point-pushforward-sheaf', Tag 00Y8, part (3): $\mathcal F_p=\mathcal F^\#_p$ for a point $p$ of a site; that a geometric point of $Y$ gives such a point of $Y_{\mathrm{proet}}$ is part of what this node asserts) and that the category of pointed neighbourhoods is nonempty and connected (it contains $(Y,\bar y)$, and two pointed neighbourhoods $(U,\bar u),(V,\bar v)$ receive maps from $(U\times_YV,(\bar u,\bar v))$, weakly etale maps being stable under base change and composition), so the colimit of the constant functor $M$ is $M$

proof.text: Put $P(U)=M$ with identity restrictions, and put $O(U)=\Lambda$ with identity restrictions. The module sheafification interface, applied to the constant presheaf of rings $O$ and its module presheaf $P$, identifies the underlying abelian sheaf of $\underline M_Y$ with the abelian sheafification $P^\#$, and identifies its unit with $P\to P^\#$. Its scalar action extends the original multiplication $(a,m)\mapsto am$. This is precisely the constant module sheaf in the statement, not a completed or condensed coefficient object.

Let $I=\mathcal N_{\bar y}^{\mathrm{op}}$ be the pointed-neighbourhood index category. The geometric stalk definition supplies its smallness in the larger universe and its filteredness; it is nonempty, containing $(Y,\bar y)$. Thus it is connected: any two objects have a common receiving object, yielding a zigzag. The restricted presheaf diagram $P$ is constant with value the additive group of $M$. The constant-connected-diagram lemma identifies its colimit with $M$; in particular the coprojection at $(Y,\bar y)$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0F6B (lemma-cofinal-etale); constant-diagram universal property as in Mathlib Limits/Connected.lean:83

proof.text: Apply preservation of geometric stalks by abelian sheafification to $P$: the map $\varinjlim_I P(U)\to\varinjlim_I P^\#(U)$ induced by the actual unit is an additive isomorphism. By Step 1 the latter colimit is the additive group of $(\underline M_Y)_{\bar y}$. Composing with the coprojection of Step 2 sends $m$ to the class of its unit image at $(Y,\bar y)$, exactly the canonical map specified in the statement. This proves additive bijectivity without presupposing that ordinary geometric points detect every pro-etale sheaf.

source.place: Tag 00Y8 (lemma-point-pushforward-sheaf), clause (3), with proetale.tex Tags 0F6B and 0F6C

proof.text: Give the stalk its $\Lambda$-action by restriction of scalars along the ring homomorphism $\Lambda\to(\Lambda_Y)_{\bar y}$ sending $a$ to the germ of $\theta_O(a)$ at $(Y,\bar y)$. For $a\in\Lambda$ and $m\in M$, represent the scalar and module germ at the same object $(Y,\bar y)$. Compatibility of the sheafification action with the presheaf action gives $\theta(am)=\theta_O(a)\theta(m)$ there, so passing to germs gives $c(am)=a c(m)$. The common-refinement definition of the stalk action is exactly this action. Hence the additive bijection $c$ of Step 3 is $\Lambda$-linear. Its inverse is linear: if $c(m)=t$, then $c(am)=at$, so $c^{-1}(at)=a c^{-1}(t)$; if $c(m)=t$ and $c(n)=u$, additivity of $c$ gives $c(m+n)=t+u$, hence $c^{-1}(t+u)=m+n=c^{-1}(t)+c^{-1}(u)$, and $c^{-1}(0)=0$ because $c(0)=0$. This is the required module isomorphism. For finite $M$, bijectivity gives a finite underlying set at every geometric point (and also preserves finite generation if finite is used in that module sense).
